question.text: When are snow and ice most dangerous, and what do slippery roads do to stopping?

answer.text: Snow and ice are at their most dangerous as they begin to melt, and slippery roads reduce tire grip and lengthen stopping distance.

teaching.text: Melting snow and ice are the most dangerous, and slick roads mean less grip and longer stops. Remember: melting ice is worst.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Snow and ice are at their most dangerous as they begin to melt, and slippery roads reduce tire grip and lengthen stopping distance.

question.text: Which spots can be icy even when the rest of the road is clear?

answer.text: Overpasses, bridges, shaded spots and snow-packed stretches can be icy even when the rest of the pavement is clear.

teaching.text: Bridges, overpasses, shade and packed snow can stay icy on an otherwise clear road. Remember: bridges freeze first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Overpasses, bridges, shaded spots and snow-packed stretches can be icy even when the rest of the pavement is clear.

question.text: Can a road that looks clear still hold icy patches?

answer.text: Bridges, overpasses and shaded spots can stay icy when the surrounding pavement is not, so a clear road can still hold icy patches.

teaching.text: A clear road can still hold icy patches in those spots. Remember: clear road, hidden ice.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bridges, overpasses and shaded spots can stay icy when the surrounding pavement is not, so a clear road can still hold icy patches.

question.text: Does four-wheel drive let you stop sooner than an ordinary car?

answer.text: Four-wheel drive improves traction but does not let a vehicle stop any sooner than an ordinary car.

teaching.text: Four-wheel drive adds traction but stops no sooner than an ordinary car. Remember: traction yes, stopping no.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Four-wheel drive improves traction but does not let a vehicle stop any sooner than an ordinary car.

question.text: What does four-wheel drive add, and what does it not add?

answer.text: Four-wheel drive adds traction but not stopping power; it cannot stop any sooner than an ordinary car.

teaching.text: Traction is not stopping power. Remember: grip, not brakes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Four-wheel drive adds traction but not stopping power; it cannot stop any sooner than an ordinary car.

question.text: What tire equipment helps in winter, and is it foolproof?

answer.text: Keep good tire tread; in winter, chains, snow tires or other traction devices are better and may be required on highways, though even these can slip on slick pavement.

teaching.text: Keep good tread; chains or snow tires help and may be required, but can still slip. Remember: chains help, not perfect.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep good tire tread; in winter, chains, snow tires or other traction devices are better and may be required on highways, though even these can slip on slick pavement.

question.text: How should your brakes be maintained?

answer.text: Keep brakes in good repair and adjusted so every wheel brakes evenly.

teaching.text: Keep brakes repaired and adjusted so every wheel brakes evenly. Remember: brakes even on every wheel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep brakes in good repair and adjusted so every wheel brakes evenly.

question.text: What should you do when traction is lost or a skid begins?

answer.text: When traction is lost or a skid begins, lift off the gas and the brake together, then steer the front wheels toward your intended path.

teaching.text: Lift off the gas and the brake together, then steer toward your path. Remember: both feet off, steer.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When traction is lost or a skid begins, lift off the gas and the brake together, then steer the front wheels toward your intended path.

question.text: How do you handle a skid in a car with anti-lock brakes?

answer.text: With anti-lock brakes, if you begin to skid, ease off the gas, press the brake and steer the front wheels the way you want to go.

teaching.text: With anti-lock brakes, ease off the gas, press the brake, and steer where you want to go. Remember: ABS: brake and steer.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With anti-lock brakes, if you begin to skid, ease off the gas, press the brake and steer the front wheels the way you want to go.

question.text: What braking technique should you use without anti-lock brakes?

answer.text: Without anti-lock brakes, use threshold braking when skidding or on slippery roads, pressing the brake to just short of locking the wheels.

teaching.text: Without anti-lock brakes, press the brake to just short of locking the wheels. Remember: brake just before lockup.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Without anti-lock brakes, use threshold braking when skidding or on slippery roads, pressing the brake to just short of locking the wheels.

question.text: Which braking technique works on any car, and which needs ABS?

answer.text: Threshold braking works on cars with or without anti-lock brakes, but anti-lock braking technique cannot be used on a car without ABS.

teaching.text: Threshold braking works on any car; the anti-lock technique needs ABS. Remember: threshold works everywhere.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Threshold braking works on cars with or without anti-lock brakes, but anti-lock braking technique cannot be used on a car without ABS.

question.text: How do skid instructions differ with and without anti-lock brakes?

answer.text: The two skid instructions differ by brakes: with anti-lock brakes you ease off the gas and push on the brake while steering, without them you use threshold braking just short of lockup.

teaching.text: Check your brakes: ABS means press and steer, no ABS means threshold braking. Remember: ABS press, non-ABS threshold.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The two skid instructions differ by brakes: with anti-lock brakes you ease off the gas and push on the brake while steering, without them you use threshold braking just short of lockup.

question.text: How does a generic skid response differ from an anti-lock skid response?

answer.text: A generic skid starts with both feet off the pedals, while an anti-lock skid adds pushing on the brake; in both, steer where you want to go.

teaching.text: A generic skid starts with both feet off; an anti-lock skid adds the brake. Remember: feet off versus brake on.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A generic skid starts with both feet off the pedals, while an anti-lock skid adds pushing on the brake; in both, steer where you want to go.

question.text: What should you do about ice, snow, frost and fogging on your windows?

answer.text: Keep defrosters and wipers working, scrape off all ice, snow and frost even for a short trip, and clear inside fogging quickly by opening a window.

teaching.text: Scrape all ice, snow and frost even for short trips, and open a window to clear fog. Remember: scrape every window.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep defrosters and wipers working, scrape off all ice, snow and frost even for a short trip, and clear inside fogging quickly by opening a window.

question.text: What lights do plows and sanding trucks flash, and how careful should you be?

answer.text: Snow plows and sanding trucks flash yellow and blue warning lights, so be extremely careful as you come up behind or go around them.

teaching.text: Plows and sanding trucks flash yellow and blue, so take extreme care around them. Remember: yellow and blue, extreme care.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Snow plows and sanding trucks flash yellow and blue warning lights, so be extremely careful as you come up behind or go around them.

question.text: When is passing a snowplow illegal?

answer.text: Use extra care near snowplows clearing snow with flashing yellow lights; passing a government-operated plow working in tandem with other plows while its yellow lights flash is illegal.

teaching.text: Passing government plows working in tandem with flashing yellow lights is illegal. Remember: never pass tandem plows.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use extra care near snowplows clearing snow with flashing yellow lights; passing a government-operated plow working in tandem with other plows while its yellow lights flash is illegal.

question.text: How should your spacing and speed change in snow and ice?

answer.text: In snow and ice keep an extra large gap behind the vehicle ahead, slow down, and give pedestrians and bicyclists extra room to get around snow and ice.

teaching.text: In snow and ice, leave an extra large gap, slow down, and give walkers and riders more room. Remember: big gap, slow down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In snow and ice keep an extra large gap behind the vehicle ahead, slow down, and give pedestrians and bicyclists extra room to get around snow and ice.

question.text: What hazards come with mountain driving, and how do you control speed downhill?

answer.text: Mountain driving brings steep grades, changing weather, bicyclists, wildlife and rocks on the road; shift to a lower gear to control speed going down steep grades.

teaching.text: Mountains bring grades, weather, riders, wildlife and rocks; use a lower gear going down. Remember: lower gear downhill.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Mountain driving brings steep grades, changing weather, bicyclists, wildlife and rocks on the road; shift to a lower gear to control speed going down steep grades.

question.text: Where is using the oncoming lane to pass illegal in the mountains?

answer.text: Using the oncoming lane to pass is illegal near the crest of a hill, on a curve or anywhere your view of oncoming traffic is blocked.

teaching.text: No passing in the oncoming lane near a crest, on a curve, or wherever your view is blocked. Remember: no pass near crests.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Using the oncoming lane to pass is illegal near the crest of a hill, on a curve or anywhere your view of oncoming traffic is blocked.

question.text: What should you expect on mountain roads besides grades and weather?

answer.text: In the mountains expect intersections hidden by trees, brush or crops, and animals on or beside the road.

teaching.text: Expect hidden intersections and animals on mountain roads. Remember: hidden crossings, animals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In the mountains expect intersections hidden by trees, brush or crops, and animals on or beside the road.

question.text: What should you do if your vehicle struggles up a steep road, and who has the right of way?

answer.text: If your vehicle struggles up a steep road, pull off at the first safe spot or keep right so others can pass; uphill vehicles have the right-of-way over downhill ones.

teaching.text: A struggling climber pulls off or keeps right, and uphill traffic has the right of way. Remember: slow climber keeps right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your vehicle struggles up a steep road, pull off at the first safe spot or keep right so others can pass; uphill vehicles have the right-of-way over downhill ones.

question.text: On a mountain grade, does the uphill or downhill vehicle have the right of way?

answer.text: On a mountain grade the uphill driver has the right-of-way, and a slow uphill vehicle should keep right or pull off to let others by.

teaching.text: On a mountain grade, uphill goes first. Remember: uphill goes first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a mountain grade the uphill driver has the right-of-way, and a slow uphill vehicle should keep right or pull off to let others by.

question.text: Which type of road has the highest death rate per mile driven?

answer.text: Rural highways are the most dangerous roads, with the highest U.S. death rate per mile driven of any road type.

teaching.text: Rural highways have the highest death rate per mile driven of any road type. Remember: rural roads are deadliest.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Rural highways are the most dangerous roads, with the highest U.S. death rate per mile driven of any road type.

question.text: What road features make rural roads risky?

answer.text: Rural roads may have sharp or blind curves, steep hills and dips, poor or hidden guide signs, narrow lanes that make passing hard, and no shoulders or guard rails.

teaching.text: Expect sharp curves, dips, hidden signs, narrow lanes and missing shoulders on rural roads. Remember: curves, dips, no shoulders.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Rural roads may have sharp or blind curves, steep hills and dips, poor or hidden guide signs, narrow lanes that make passing hard, and no shoulders or guard rails.

question.text: What hazards should you expect on rural roads?

answer.text: On rural roads expect blind driveways, T-intersections and side streets hidden by plants, plus rocks, debris, animals, crossing farm vehicles, unmarked railroad crossings and slow or small vehicles like bicycles.

teaching.text: Watch for blind driveways, animals, farm vehicles and unmarked railroad crossings. Remember: hidden driveways, farm vehicles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On rural roads expect blind driveways, T-intersections and side streets hidden by plants, plus rocks, debris, animals, crossing farm vehicles, unmarked railroad crossings and slow or small vehicles like bicycles.

question.text: How do rural road surfaces affect your control?

answer.text: Rural pavement is often rough or unpaved dirt and gravel with less traction, and washboarding on gravel roads can upset steering and control.

teaching.text: Gravel and dirt mean less traction, and washboarding can upset steering. Remember: gravel means less grip.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Rural pavement is often rough or unpaved dirt and gravel with less traction, and washboarding on gravel roads can upset steering and control.

question.text: What can potholes do to your vehicle?

answer.text: Potholes can make the vehicle bounce or jolt and cause the tires to lose traction.

teaching.text: Potholes can jolt the car and cost the tires traction. Remember: potholes steal traction.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Potholes can make the vehicle bounce or jolt and cause the tires to lose traction.

question.text: Why are rural roads dangerous for bicyclists, and how should you pass them?

answer.text: Many bicyclist deaths happen on rural roads because of higher speeds, so slow down and give more than the required three feet when passing riders there, since dangerous wind blasts can lead to riders being struck.

teaching.text: On rural roads, slow down and give bicyclists more than three feet. Remember: more than three feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Many bicyclist deaths happen on rural roads because of higher speeds, so slow down and give more than the required three feet when passing riders there, since dangerous wind blasts can lead to riders being struck.

question.text: What do work zones contain, and how are changes announced?

answer.text: Work zones contain equipment and workers and may change routes daily, and signs, cones and other devices placed ahead warn of the changes.

teaching.text: Work zones change often, and signs and cones ahead warn of the changes. Remember: signs warn of changes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Work zones contain equipment and workers and may change routes daily, and signs, cones and other devices placed ahead warn of the changes.

question.text: How should you drive in a work zone?

answer.text: In a work zone stay alert, be ready to stop suddenly and never tailgate.

teaching.text: Stay alert, be ready to stop, and never tailgate in a work zone. Remember: alert, ready, no tailgating.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a work zone stay alert, be ready to stop suddenly and never tailgate.

question.text: What can large projects use, and why are speed limits lowered?

answer.text: Large projects may use flaggers, portable concrete barriers, complex signs and reduced speed limits, and those lower limits give drivers more time to read and react.

teaching.text: Lower work-zone limits give you more time to read and react. Remember: lower limits, more time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Large projects may use flaggers, portable concrete barriers, complex signs and reduced speed limits, and those lower limits give drivers more time to read and react.

question.text: Why must work-zone crews watch traffic constantly?

answer.text: Work-zone crews cannot be fully separated from traffic and must watch constantly for drivers who drift into the work area.

teaching.text: Crews cannot be fully separated from traffic, so they watch for drifting drivers. Remember: crews cannot be walled off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Work-zone crews cannot be fully separated from traffic and must watch constantly for drivers who drift into the work area.

question.text: What happens to fines and enforcement in work zones?

answer.text: Police enforcement is often added in work zones, and fines are doubled there as they are in school zones.

teaching.text: Work-zone fines are doubled, just like school-zone fines. Remember: work zone fines double.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Police enforcement is often added in work zones, and fines are doubled there as they are in school zones.

question.text: What causes most work-zone crashes, and what should you obey?

answer.text: In a work zone, obey work-zone speed signs and flaggers, and watch the vehicle ahead, because most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions caused by inattention.

teaching.text: Most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions from inattention. Remember: inattention causes rear-enders.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a work zone, obey work-zone speed signs and flaggers, and watch the vehicle ahead, because most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions caused by inattention.

question.text: Which zones share doubled fines, and what is the most common work-zone crash?

answer.text: Work-zone and school-zone fines are both doubled, and most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions.

teaching.text: Doubled fines and rear-end crashes define work-zone risk. Remember: double fines, rear-end crashes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Work-zone and school-zone fines are both doubled, and most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions.

question.text: Why should you drive defensively?

answer.text: You cannot count on others obeying every rule, so drive calmly, ignore aggressive drivers and practice defensive driving.

teaching.text: Others may break rules, so drive calmly and defensively and ignore aggressive drivers. Remember: expect others to slip.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You cannot count on others obeying every rule, so drive calmly, ignore aggressive drivers and practice defensive driving.

question.text: Who in the vehicle must wear a seat belt?

answer.text: Make sure every person in the vehicle wears a seat belt.

teaching.text: Everyone in the vehicle wears a seat belt. Remember: everyone buckles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Make sure every person in the vehicle wears a seat belt.

question.text: When does Colorado law allow mobile device use while driving?

answer.text: Colorado law bars using a mobile device while driving except to contact police or fire services, in an emergency, or with a hands-free accessory.

teaching.text: Phone use while driving is allowed only for police, fire, emergencies or hands-free. Remember: hands-free or emergency only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Colorado law bars using a mobile device while driving except to contact police or fire services, in an emergency, or with a hands-free accessory.

question.text: When does Colorado law allow texting while driving?

answer.text: Colorado law bars texting while driving except to contact police or fire services or in an emergency; the listed texting exceptions do not include a hands-free accessory.

teaching.text: Texting while driving is allowed only for police, fire or emergencies, with no hands-free exception. Remember: no texting, even hands-free.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Colorado law bars texting while driving except to contact police or fire services or in an emergency; the listed texting exceptions do not include a hands-free accessory.

question.text: Which law has a hands-free exception, and which does not?

answer.text: Hand-held phone use has a hands-free exception, but texting does not; both allow contacting police or fire and emergencies.

teaching.text: Hands-free covers calls but never texts. Remember: calls hands-free, texts never.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand-held phone use has a hands-free exception, but texting does not; both allow contacting police or fire and emergencies.

question.text: Where should your hands be on the wheel, and how should you turn?

answer.text: Keep both hands on the wheel at eight and four or nine and three o'clock, turn with the hand-over-hand or push-pull-slide method, and never palm the wheel or let it slide through your fingers after a turn.

teaching.text: Keep hands at eight and four or nine and three, and never let the wheel slide back on its own. Remember: hands low, never palm.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep both hands on the wheel at eight and four or nine and three o'clock, turn with the hand-over-hand or push-pull-slide method, and never palm the wheel or let it slide through your fingers after a turn.

question.text: How should you scan, and how do you look at intersections?

answer.text: Scan ahead, to the sides and behind, and always look left, right and left again when turning at, crossing or entering an intersection, watching for pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists.

teaching.text: Scan all around and look left, right and left again at intersections. Remember: left, right, left again.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Scan ahead, to the sides and behind, and always look left, right and left again when turning at, crossing or entering an intersection, watching for pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists.

question.text: How far ahead should you look down the road?

answer.text: Look at least ten seconds down the road, about one block in the city or half a mile on the open road, to avoid last-second braking or swerving.

teaching.text: Look at least ten seconds ahead to avoid last-second braking or swerving. Remember: look far ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Look at least ten seconds down the road, about one block in the city or half a mile on the open road, to avoid last-second braking or swerving.

question.text: How often should you check your rearview mirror?

answer.text: Check your rearview mirror every five to eight seconds, more often in heavy traffic, and especially when changing lanes, slowing, backing, leaving an intersection or going down a long or steep hill.

teaching.text: Check the rearview mirror every five to eight seconds, more in heavy traffic. Remember: mirror every few seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check your rearview mirror every five to eight seconds, more often in heavy traffic, and especially when changing lanes, slowing, backing, leaving an intersection or going down a long or steep hill.

question.text: How does the three-second rule work?

answer.text: Under normal conditions use the three-second rule: when the car ahead passes a fixed point, count three seconds, and if you reach the point first you are following too closely.

teaching.text: Count three seconds from a fixed point; reaching it first means you are too close. Remember: count to three.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under normal conditions use the three-second rule: when the car ahead passes a fixed point, count three seconds, and if you reach the point first you are following too closely.

question.text: What are the three different times that guide your eyes and spacing?

answer.text: Three different times guide your eyes and spacing: look ten seconds ahead, check the mirror every five to eight seconds, and leave three seconds behind the car ahead.

teaching.text: Ten seconds ahead, five to eight between mirror checks, three seconds behind. Remember: ten ahead, mirror, three behind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Three different times guide your eyes and spacing: look ten seconds ahead, check the mirror every five to eight seconds, and leave three seconds behind the car ahead.
